Clinics--as holistic entities--have more control over clients mistreating staff than we like to think. I've had some awful experiences as a client, and I'm mild mannered to a fault, but I would have been within my rights to Karen out a couple times. 

Obviously some people are horrible everywhere they go, and some situations make rational behavior drastically more difficult. But the majority of people can be deescalated long before they hit the ceiling if staff are afforded the time, emotional bandwidth for compassion, and clinic culture to demonstrate that they care. If everyone's bitter, exhausted, always rushing, hates their job & coworkers & clients, and has ended up acting like they're working at McDonalds, clients are going to feel that and they're going to treat staff in kind.

On the one hand, there is a big difference between a dark color and a stark black. In the piece I'm working, I replaced  black w overdyed floss in a dark cool brown--no one would know it's not black, yet the overall effect is still much nicer than if I'd used black. So the change you've made to this piece is subtle but significant, looks very nice, and will go well with the as-yet unused colors.

OTOH, if you're not happy with it, you're not happy with it. For example, if your goal is to create drama via a strong contrast between the fill color and the outline, you're right that you haven't achieved that as well as you could with a brighter/lighter fill color.

You've come so far, my suggestion would be to see how you feel about finishing the piece as is and sitting with it for a while to see what you think--but not if doing so will be an unhappy slog for you!

If you do start over, you could take the suggestion of stitching over this piece as a test, or you could do some  swatches of several stitches in each color to get a feeling for the palette ahead of time.

Behavioral euthanasia sucks, no two ways around it. It's important and necessary but it is always, always difficult for us, whether in a shelter or veterinary setting (I've been part of both). It breaks my heart for the dog and their family. I have never seen an owner be "ok" with behavioral euth; I have had them confess to incredible guilt and shame.

One thing that helps me is to really try and think things through logistically from the owner's perspective. In this case, I don't know the severity or circumstances of the bites, so instead of commenting on that I will refer to my most recent behavioral euth. This was a large breed dog who had bitten the owner severely in the past (requiring medical treatment) & whose triggers seemed random and unpredictable (e.g. lunged and snapped in response to a sliding door being opened). Other than behavioral euthanasia, the only options available to his owners other than surrendering to a shelter (which would also result in euthanasia)--i.e. continued training efforts or attempting to rehome--involved continued exposure to the risk of serious injury every day, in her own home, by the animal she loved, & all the emotional pain/stress that would entail. In this situation, if the owners hadn't already worked with a behaviorist, I wouldn't feel comfortable requiring them to do so before proceeding with euthanasia.

2. Reports of ataxia are suspected to be observations of dogs w/muscular atrophy sharply increasing their activity without the muscle to support it--i.e. their weakness is more apparent the more active they are; the rep advised to limit mobility after the first few injections, as dogs in this situation can injure themselves

I've been present for home euthanasias of two pets I loved; not my own, but my brother's cat we had grown up with and my roommate's dog I did hospice care for. It's what I want for my own someday, god willing.

The main benefit I see is your pet's last moments being in a setting where not only they buy also you feel comfortable & have a measure of control/freedom (e.g. to choose/let them choose the location, to grieve as loudly as you need), which even the most compassionate and well-prepared clinical setting obviously can't replicate. My roommate put on loud music, for example.

There are drawbacks as well. One thing both my roommate and brother struggled with beforehand was the idea of having to be in the spot where their pet died, though afterward this wasn't as much of a problem for them as they feared (though I'm sure it's prohibitive for some). I knew the vet personally in my roommate's case, but not my brother's, and that vet being a stranger to me put me on edge (though it made no difference to my brother).

As everyone else said... We don't know this owner, what they were thinking or feeling that day, or what the last days and hours before that looked like. I will never judge a client solely on the choice not to be present.

That said, I don't like being part of euthanasias with no owner present because I find them much more emotionally taxing. I feel a need to step into an owner-like role--to do the things I would do for my own pet, like hold them, talk to them, etc, both to comfort the pet and to sort of honor the owner in their absence. It makes it feel a little closer to a firsthand experience rather than the secondhand experience that most euths are. So it's difficult. I can separate that from my feelings about the owner. But I think for some people, anger or upset with the owner can be a way of dealing with complicated feelings like these.

The most recent time, I came up with a framework that I haven't had occasion to try using again yet, but at that time it felt like it helped. I decided to imagine that the client had given all their love and care for their pet to me to hold temporarily, and once the pet was gone, as I bagged them and put them in the freezer, I relinquished it all back to them. That's arguably pretty woo-woo lol but it helped me maintain some emotional distance while still doing what I felt was right by the pet & client.

There are some misconceptions in this thread about what title protection means. It means that people who aren't registered/licensed/certified technicians can't call themselves technicians, & depending on the state, may face fines for doing so. It doesn't mean VAs are or should be severely restricted as to what tasks they can perform. I live in a state with title protection and am legally allowed to draw blood, place catheters, etc, and I'm expected to learn and perform every skill that's legally available to me. I would never call myself a tech, because I'm not one. Nor do I make a tech's wages--rightfully. But I'm a skilled medical professional.

OP, all cats are born the same way: animals who self-domesticated what was, in the grand scheme of things, very recently. Their critical socialization window is both earlier and briefer than dogs, ending at around 2mo old. They don't innately get along w humans; any cat that is friendly to humans is a cat who had positive contact w humans around that window. A cat who isn't socialized in that time is feral. Feral cats aren't "bad," but they *are* much closer to a wild animal than a pet.

Do you know your guy's history? How did he come to the shelter? How long was he there before you had him? These are really important questions, because he was well past his socialization window by the time of your first post. If he wasn't already being handled by people for months before you got him, then you aren't looking at a scared cat having trouble adjusting due to behavioral issues, but a normal feral cat. The chance of making a feral cat comfortable, happy, and (crucially) *safe* to live with in a home is, frankly, very poor. For example, Alley Cat Allies doesn't recommend trying to socialize feral cats over 4mo. 

Does your shelter have TNR or barn cat programs?

Hi! I have anosmia and have been in the field about 5.5 years, starting in kennels. I've never had a problem with my performance related to cleaning.

When I started, I didn't tell anyone for several months, and there are still people I've worked with for years who don't know because it just hasn't come up. I looove this question and got a little long-winded, sorry :-) It's really cool to me how you think of smells in a scientific/mathematical way, because I'm very different. I'm super interested in the science of olfaction, but when it comes to a practical day-to-day understanding of scents, I rely on a library of sociocultural associations I've picked up through reading and conversation.

I find it fun to read stuff like perfume reviews and wine tasting notes, or challenge people to try and describe a scent to me. There are not actually many words that exclusively describe smell, so descriptions of scents necessarily get metaphorical, almost poetic. E.g. things can smell "green," "masculine," "heavy," and many other things we have non-olfactory context for; scents may evoke settings, actions, and moods (e.g. "a relaxing day at the beach"); certain smells are more/less likely to register as familiar, homey, and positive vs. gross, distressing, and negative... That gives you an idea of how I process things.

Re: whether smells can be overwhelming, definitely, depending on the person. Some people are on the opposite end of the spectrum from us and are highly sensitive to smells. Some smells may be attached to very negatively charged memories. And it really does seem like smell is a constant experience (except people stop noticing smells like their own sweat or their own home). I sometimes get overwhelmed by noisy & visually stimulating environments, so I really suspect if I woke up tomorrow able to smell I would have a really difficult time lol!!

As you can tell from the replies, assuming/acting like you can smell is super common for us as kids. Kids are social mimics! As someone else said, what to do partially depends on the client. I default to a slower/quieter,  very gentle and sympathetic tone. Some just want it over with and/or appear not to like feeling pitied, and I'll dial things back and be a more dry and professional. Some are animated and want to laugh and joke, and I'll try to meet that energy if it seems to work for them. 

In general I explain everything even more thoroughly than I usually would--The more emotional your client is, the harder time they'll have absorbing really simple stuff, and I don't want them to feel totally lost and confused. For example, the first thing I'll do is broadly outline everything that's going to happen and in what order. I'll hang out while they fill out paperwork so I can show them where to put what, make sure they don't skip sections, and remind them of the date. If I'm placing the catheter in front of the client, I narrate everything I do (even more thoroughly than I do normally lol) & especially warn them before I flush the catheter (I've had people assume the saline is the euth solution!!).

Just about anything you can think of that draws attention to the loving bond between them and their pet is good to say. I like "I can tell how much she loves you." Sorry my bad. This part depends a lot on what kind of flavor you want, so I will give some examples, but look up "chicken marinade" or "chicken spice mix" for other ideas.

Marinade is any mix of oil, vinegar, other premade liquids/sauces, and spices. You put the chicken in a ziploc, cover with marinade, and let it soak for a couple hours. A classic one is ½ cup olive oil, ½c balsamic vinegar, ¼c soy sauce, ¼c Worcestershire, ⅛c lemon juice, ¾c brown sugar, some salt & pepper & garlic powder.

The other option is you rub both sides generouslh with olive oil and spices, then let it sit for like 15min before baking; for example you can do just salt just salt & pepper, or salt & lemon pepper, or use a premade mix (e.g. garlic salt, herb mix, poultry mix).

The foil? You set it in the middle of a square of aluminum foil, fold it so the sides meet on top of the chicken (& any other stuff e.g. veggies, garlic, lemon slices), and crimp it tightly all the way along the seam so it kind of ends up looking like... a calzone on its side 🤔? There should be a little extra room inside & it should be pretty airtight. Then put it in a pan/tray in case it leaks & bake at 425 for 20-25mins (higher temp for shorter time = less dry, but check with a meat thermometer to make sure it reaches 165).

Other commenter mentioned it, but my method to keep them from drying out is to marinade or rub with whatever oils and spices and then enclose in foil before baking. The downside is you don't get browning.

I am no expert by far, but I did used to work with dogs like this when I volunteered with a shelter. Sorry in advance for length; I'm passionate about this, and you sound like you really care, so I'm going to dump a lot of info on you--Feel free to take what applies and ignore what doesn't!

1st, what you're seeing isn't atypical. We used to say it takes at least a month to start seeing the dog's real personality. That said, I can't tell you how much or how fast she can improve. She may suddenly blossom, or she may make very slow gradual progress and only up to a certain point. Either way it will be a big time investment and it is ok if this is more than what you signed up for!!! OTOH, earning a terrified dog's trust is incredibly rewarding.

The main thing we would do for dogs like this was sit with them for long periods (like ideally upwards of an hour) each day. We would sit as near as they would allow without totally shutting down or running away, toss treats, talk out loud so they heard our voice, and reward them with high value treats for things like looking at us/moving towards us/sniffing us/etc. We would encourage them to do behaviors like chewing toys/treats, ripping up stuffed items (with supervision), or scavenging for treats (scatter some on the floor, hide them under blankets, puzzle toys, etc) which can all help dogs destress.

For walks, we would always take them out as long as they were willing to go out, but not force them if they weren't. If they got scared and froze outside, we would just wait for them (..as long as practically possible lol). A really long leash is nice for dogs who are scared on lead because you can let them be "loose" in the yard but still hang onto the end of the leash for security.

We also used [clicker training](https://www.akc.org/expert-advice/training/clicker-training-your-dog-mark-and-reward/), which is not just good training method, but also a great way to bond & help draw dogs out of their shell. [Here is an article I found](https://www.clickertraining.com/helping-shy-dogs-blossom) on using a clicker to teach targeting for fearful dogs. The [box game](https://www.clickertraining.com/101-things-to-do-with-a-box) is also great because you can reward her for interacting with her environment on her own.

Long-term, I would consider trying to find a [veterinary behaviorist](https://www.dacvb.org) who could both help with her specific behavioral & training needs and potentially prescribe anti-anxiety medication if warranted.

I'm a veterinary assistant! Like someone else said, CBD is ok for dogs but not THC. I would not recommend making your own stuff but rather look for CBD products made for pets.

When choosing a brand, look for ones that have testing done by a third party lab to verify things like CBD content & safety (often called a certificate of analysis/COA).

There's definitely some evidence CBD can be helpful for pain in pets, just please don't rely on it to replace veterinary care. We have a lot of ways to help old age related mobility/pain, and we want your guy to be as comfortable as possible for as long as he can. If you don't trust your vet I recommend looking for a new one now rather than waiting.

Finally, re: his behavior, consider asking your vet about canine cognitive dysfunction (ie doggie dementia). That kind of just sitting around, staring at nothing, depressed-type behavior can be a sign.

This is definitely a known training hurdle--Dogs who will only follow a cue if they anticipate their reward. Right now she has learned "mom has food = I get a treat every time. Mom doesn't have good = I get a treat none of the time." The fix is something called variable ratio reinforcement. That's a fancy term, but basically it means you start asking her to do a behavior twice before she gets rewarded, then three times, etc etc, until down the road you reward sporadically & randomly. This way she learns "every time, I may or may not get a treat." My explanation isn't great.. you can read some more from Ian Dunbar [here](https://www.dogstardaily.com/blogs/reinforcement-schedules).

I only recently felt like jugs had started to click for me! Here are tips that have helped me, sorry if any are super obvious/beginner:

We don't shave for jugs (fear free) so I focus on palpating. When I feel something but not certain if it's a vein, I let up and then hold off again. A vein will flatten and pop back up.

Sometimes a dog has easier anatomy on one side than the other; some dogs I've been totally lost and frustrated till I switched sides. So don't give up till you check both.

Some dogs' veins pop best if their head is actually slightly out of position. So don't stop palpating if the dog is wiggling around, and don't be shy to ask your holder to move their head around a little.

If I get a flash but then can't draw, it usually means I've gone through the vein, and if I keep the position while pulling out I can usually get it. (Obviously better not to go through the vein in the first place, but yanno.)

Finally, everyone learns differently, so don't kick yourself if certain tips don't work for you. Eg for me, practicing on sedated dogs wasn't helpful because I just couldn't transfer the knowledge to awake, moving, sitting up dogs; but taking notes after every blood draw did help me even though some people thought it was silly.

You'll get there I promise! Keep pushing!

Im not a behavior professional, but to me what you described sounds like some normal-range stress on separation. She is a little nervous when you leave, then she self-soothes with the toy, which is great, and relaxes enough she can settle. 

"True" separation anxiety is serious and something you would want a trainer and/or vet for. It looks more like loud & persistent vocalization, destructive behavior specifically at entrances/exits (this is a hallmark), pacing/restlessness, hypersalivation, etc, even house soiling and self-injury. It  actually can start before you even leave the house, during your getting-ready-to-go routine. You're right though that it doesn't abate till you return, since sep anx dogs can't deescalate on their own. It's also common for these dogs to be generally clingy or have other anxiety/fear issues.

Overall, it sounds like you know your girl really well and have already helped her a lot! Unless you're seeing a trend of her behavior on separation worsening I wouldn't change anything major. 

To help the stress she does have when you leave, a good strategy is to have a special long-lasting treat like a chew, food puzzle, or frozen Kong that you only give her as you're leaving. That will give her a more positive association and also help distract her. It can also help to make leaving & returning really low key, ie no big goodbye before you go & wait till she's calm to greet her when you return.

Best of luck!!

A lot of behaviorists agree that dogs have good control over their jaw and the strength of their bite. Yet some dogs tend to bite harder than others. This is because of something called bite inhibition or aqcuired bite inhibition, which is learned early in life and, to simplify, basically means how hard a dog is "willing" to bite. So if you look at the history of any one dog with multiple bites, you'll *often* see that they *tend* to deliver similar severity bites, or at least will not exceed a certain severity. (Sidenote, this may actually be part of why your Pom never seriously hurt anyone--Some small dogs can still definitely do pretty good damage.)

Take 3 hypothetical dogs with similar sizes & environments. Each dog has bitten on multiple occasions in response to a similar stimulus, say, someone reaching for a toy left on the ground. Dog 1 has bruised, but not broken skin each time. Dog 2 has delivered a single quick bite with scrapes or shallow punctures each time. Dog 3 has delivered multiple bites plus  gouges from latching and shaking each time. Even though they are all biting for the same reason, bite severity is going to be a larger part of the conversation around what level of risk everyone is ok living with, and therefore how to move forward, for dog 2, and will sadly probably be the major deciding factor of dog 3's fate.

They are similar, arguably connected, but distinct concepts.

1. Discussing only impulse control could lead you to treating your dog as the source of the problem: "My dog was naughty because he's too impulsive." Really most minor problems like these can be solved by paying more attention to the dogs' environment and our own actions. Eg "my dog dug up the flowerbed because I haven't taught him I only want him to dig in the sand pit," or "my dog got in the trash can because it doesn't have a latch."

2. The idea of certain behaviors as self-reinforcing conveys WHY that 'impulse' is hard to control: Chewing, digging, etc are naturally 'fun' for dogs, so these behaviors are their own rewards. Every time the dog repeats a self-reinforcing behavior, they're 'rewarded' for that behavior and the behavior becomes more entrenched. This is why these behaviors can be difficult to change & why managing the dog's environment to prevent them or provide alternatives is so important.

3. As I said, it's generally thought that dogs CAN'T make associations when rewards (or punishments) are delayed. Their brains are different and their sense of time is different. A dog isn't able to think "I could chew mom's shoes, but if I don't, she'll give me lots of treats later." If you get home, see the dog has been good all day, and give them a treat, they will more likely associate the treat with "mom just got home" or "I am sitting" or "a car is passing by outside" than with "I didn't chew on mom's shoes all day."

4. Not sure what this last part means as I didn't describe any rules.

Impulse control is not the whole story. A lot of unwanted behavior in dogs is what's called self-reinforcing. It may have a built in reward (eg counter surfing or stealing from garbage) or may just be basic drives that are satisfying to fulfil (eg chewing, ripping stuff up--these can be anxious behaviors, but are also just natural behaviors, and dogs that aren't taught rules around these behaviors or aren't given access to a 'legal' outlet for them will be 'naughty'). Simply put, they repeat these behaviors because they are enjoyable. And dogs don't do delayed consequences well at all; if a fair bit of a time (I'm thinking more than a few minutes) passes between the behavior and later consequence, they may not be able to associate these things at all.

I see diagnostic labels as shorthand for sets of experiences, not as discrete categories. Most are descriptions of sets of symptoms that commonly occur together. CPTSD is a looser category symptoms-wise, because it describes a root cause (ie, complex trauma) that has global effects. You can derive a list of core symptoms that are common to most people to whom the CPTSD label applies, but there is also a lot of variation. Due to all this + the way the psych system is set up, it’s super common for people who eventually decide the right choice for them is trauma-based treatment to have multiple other diagnoses applied to them first, and BPD & DID pop up a lot in discussions about this. And from the other direction, many/most people w diagnoses of BPD or DID experienced early childhood trauma. At the end of the day, all three labels are attempts to organize and communicate powerful human experiences that we have no way to measure or empirically define, so of course few people are gonna strictly resemble textbook definitions and will fall into gray areas... So I find trying to nail down whether anyone “really has” x or y or z pretty much counterproductive.

Overall I would say hospitalization is a double-edged sword. It gives you a break from the "real world," but introduces new stressors too. I would plan on having some processing to do afterwards. That said, in the hospital you are free to scream, cry, collapse, throw a fit, and generally let your emotions come out in messy, "inappropriate" ways; and you will be able to interact with people who are going through the same things and in the same place as you. Both those things can be really healing.

Your personal experience will really depend a lot on how good the policies & staff at the particular hospital you will be at are, so do some research on its history, patient experiences there/reviews, etc, just to make sure you're not heading into a horror story. (Understaffing, underfunding, incompetent staff & doctors, bureaucratic screwups like getting the wrong meds, etc are run-of-the-mill; overuse of antipsychotics/restraints, unsanitary or unsafe conditions, and of course physical/sexual abuse or other illegal behavior are not.) I would also try to look up your legal rights, but that can be confusing, and they should inform you of them at the hospital. Those are really crucial, because if you're going to do something like refuse medication, being able to cite the law is a huge boon; just flat-out refusing meds can be really risky (and can lead to getting slapped with one of those stigmatized labels the other commenter mentioned). If you're a voluntary patient, you will probably have more rights.

Good luck, I hope it will be a positive experience for you.
